title: Blocking in Async Code

writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
A blocking call occupies an executor worker without yielding, so unrelated tasks can stall. Move CPU-heavy or blocking work to a dedicated pool and await its result.

An executor worker can poll many async tasks because each task yields while waiting for nonblocking I/O. A synchronous `sleep`, filesystem call, expensive compression loop, or blocking foreign-library call can occupy that worker instead. Other ready tasks then wait even though they could run. Putting `async` on a function signature does not change a blocking call inside it into cooperative work.

Use the runtime's blocking pool or a dedicated worker thread for truly blocking operations, and pass owned input into it. The offload has overhead, so a tiny calculation may be cheaper to perform directly; measure the latency of other tasks under realistic load. CPU-heavy jobs can saturate even a blocking pool, so consider a bounded queue or a separate compute service when throughput matters. Think about shutdown too: a blocking call may not stop simply because its async caller was cancelled.

Create one task that repeatedly awaits a short timer and logs the delay. Alongside it, run a second task with a long synchronous sleep. Observe the timer stalls when both compete for an executor worker, then move the blocking operation to the runtime's blocking facility and compare. Change the sleep to a CPU loop and watch the same scheduling issue. Keep track of where the result and error travel back to the async caller. The goal is predictable responsiveness, not merely making code compile inside an async block.
